doc.title: Phil Woods interviewed by Monk Rowe, Delaware Water Gap, PA, November 8, 1999

title: His tone and natural embouchure
summary: Woods says his tone is a gift, helped by natural embouchure, breathing and musical parents.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: You have a tone that’s pretty recognized I’d have to say.

I think so. I think God blessed me with that, I do believe that’s something you can work on to a certain degree, but if you’re born with a bad tone you’re probably going to have a © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-
bad tone. I think I was put on this earth to play the saxophone. I think my build, my physiogn-omy is kind of made to be a saxophone player. It didn’t occur to me until much later.

I think so, yeah. For whatever it’s worth. I believe in fate in that aspect of it. Because I could always get a good sound. I didn’t have to work at it, although I did a lot of long tones. But I got a good tone right from the beginning. I was lucky. I was blessed with a natural embouchure. I never had to scuffle with it, I never tightened up here, I always breathed from the diaphragm, the pitch was pretty well centered, and that’s something that’s in the genes. I think that comes from your parents and all that. And my parents loved music and I think it shows.
Some little quote I remember from one critic and they commented on your placement in bebop and that you played more in tune than almost all of them.
It’s a nice thing to — yeah, I appreciate that support.
